vignette:
When she is 29, she is living in a city that is slowly being remade by war. At first, she tells herself that ordinary life can continue. She goes to work, carries groceries home, edits manuscripts late into the evening, and learns to pause whenever she hears a distant boom, waiting to see if it is thunder or artillery. She is already working as an editor then, trained to notice small inconsistencies, awkward phrasing, the one sentence in a page that does not belong. During those months, the same careful attention turns outward. She notices which streets are suddenly empty, which neighbors stop opening their curtains, how people lower their voices when they speak about disappearances.

One afternoon, the war reaches her directly. She is on her way back from the office carrying marked-up pages in a satchel when shelling begins without warning. The first blast throws her to the ground. Glass breaks above her, and she remembers the strange detail of paper fluttering into the street like white birds. A second explosion lands closer. She crawls toward the recessed doorway of a pharmacy with several other civilians. A man beside her is bleeding from the neck. Someone is screaming for a child. She can smell dust, gasoline, something metallic that she later understands is blood. She does not know how long she remains there, pressed against cold stone, certain each incoming sound is the one that will kill her. When the shelling stops, the street she knows is no longer recognizable. She walks home shaking, passing bodies covered with coats and fragments of buildings she used to enter every week.

After that day, fear becomes the structure of her life. She sleeps in her clothes. She keeps a bag by the door with documents, bread, and family photographs. At night she lies awake listening for engines, for boots, for the whistling descent that gave only seconds of warning. If she dozes, she jolts awake with her heart racing, already halfway to the floor before she knows where she is. She begins avoiding the route where the shelling happened, then avoids the market, then any street with open intersections. Her world narrows to whatever feels least exposed.

She eventually leaves the country with relatives. The leaving itself is hurried and guilty; she survives by going, while others cannot. In the new country, people tell her she is safe now, and she understands that intellectually. Her body does not believe them. She startles at buses backfiring. Construction noise empties her mind. On the Fourth of July, when fireworks begin, she locks herself in the bathroom and sits on the floor with her hands over her ears, ashamed of how quickly she has disappeared from the present.

Years pass. She builds a life that from the outside looks steady. She marries, later divorces, raises a son, and returns fully to editorial work. Colleagues know her as exacting and reliable, the kind of editor who can hold the architecture of a book in her head and hear the false note in a paragraph immediately. She likes the control of the work, the way language can be revised until it behaves. But war keeps leaking into the room. If an author describes an explosion, rubble, detention, or flight, she feels her chest tighten before she has finished the line. She tells herself to be professional and keeps going, though she often realizes she has read the same sentence five times without taking in the words.

Now, at 66, she lives alone in a quiet apartment and still scans every room when she enters. She chooses seats near exits in cafés and restaurants. She dislikes having her back to windows. She keeps the television volume low because sudden noise feels like an assault. Sleep is unreliable. Some nights she dreams she is back in that doorway, unable to move, trying to make herself smaller while the air shakes around her. On those mornings she wakes drenched in sweat, disoriented and furious that after so many years, her first sensation is still danger.

She does not speak easily about the war. For a long time she tells her family only the broad outline: it was bad, many people died, she was lucky. In sessions, what emerges instead are fragments and sensory pieces-the white flutter of pages, the smell of burning, the man's hand at his throat. She often apologizes after crying, as if she has broken a rule. She says she should be over it by now. She compares herself unfavorably to others who "went through worse." Yet her days remain organized around not feeling too much. She avoids news footage from conflict zones, skips public celebrations with fireworks, and turns down invitations to crowded events. Even pleasure has to pass through a calculation of safety.

What troubles her most is how war has shaped her sense of time. Part of her knows she is an older woman in a peaceful city, working at her desk with a cup of coffee and a manuscript open in front of her. Another part is still in that street, waiting for the next blast. She says she has had a good life in many ways, and she means it. But she also says that some portion of her has never fully come home.
